related_questions.question: Is COVID worse the second time you get it?

text_blocks.snippet: It's difficult to definitively say if a second COVID-19 infection is worse than the first. Emerging data suggests that subsequent infections are often milder due to prior immunity and potentially less severe circulating variants. However, some individuals, particularly those with compromised immune systems, older adults, or those who experienced severe initial infections, may experience more severe symptoms with repeat infections, according to Jefferson Health and the University of Nebraska Medical Center. There's also the concern of potential long-term impacts, such as worsened long COVID symptoms, on the heart, lungs, and brain with repeat infections, says Jefferson Health.

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, it is possible to get COVID-19 more than once. Reinfection with the virus that causes COVID-19 occurs when someone is infected, recovers, and then gets infected again. While a previous infection can offer some protection against reinfection, it's not a guarantee, and the level of protection can decrease over time. Additionally, new variants of the virus can emerge with the ability to evade existing immunity.

list.title: Immunity wanes:
list.snippet: The protection from a previous infection doesn't last forever. The immune response can weaken over time, leaving individuals susceptible to reinfection.

list.title: New variants:
list.snippet: The virus is constantly evolving, and new variants can emerge that are better at evading the body's immune defenses.

list.title: Individual immune responses:
list.snippet: People with weakened immune systems may not develop a strong or long-lasting immune response to the virus, making them more vulnerable to reinfection.

text_blocks.snippet: Even after a previous infection, individuals can still experience severe illness from a reinfection. Staying up-to-date on vaccinations and seeking treatment when symptoms start can help reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization, according to the CDC.
